summary: Wisdom speaks in the first person, describing her origin from the Most High, her reach through creation, and her appointed dwelling in Jacob, Israel, Zion, and Jerusalem. The poem then pictures Wisdom as trees, fragrances, fruit, honey, rivers, and overflowing water. The chapter closes by identifying these things with the covenant law of Moses and with the teacher’s ongoing work of instruction for all who seek wisdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter is a hinge in Sirach: Wisdom is not only practical skill but is located in Israel’s worship, covenant, and instruction. It joins cosmic language about Wisdom with the concrete book of the law and the work of teaching.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers who wanted instruction shaped by the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with the temple and priesthood central to worship and Jewish scribes teaching within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in poetic form, here especially a hymn-like self-praise of personified Wisdom followed by reflection on Torah and teaching.

outline.heading: Wisdom Speaks Among Her People
outline.note: Wisdom is introduced as praising herself and speaking in the congregation of the Most High.

outline.heading: Wisdom From Creation To Israel
outline.note: Wisdom says she came from the Most High, moved through heaven, sea, earth, peoples, and nations, then was commanded to dwell in Jacob and take root in Israel, Zion, and Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Wisdom As Trees, Fragrance, And Fruit
outline.note: Wisdom is compared with lofty trees, fragrant spices, tabernacle incense, branches, vines, flowers, glory, and riches; verse 18 is blank in the World English Bible.

outline.heading: Wisdom Invites Desire And Obedience
outline.note: Wisdom calls those who desire her to come, eat, drink, obey, and work with her.

outline.heading: Wisdom And The Covenant Law
outline.note: The speaker identifies these things with the book of the covenant and the law commanded by Moses; verse 24 is blank in the World English Bible.

outline.heading: Wisdom As Abundant Waters
outline.note: Wisdom and understanding are compared with great rivers, harvest abundance, light, the sea, and the great deep.

outline.heading: The Teacher’s Overflowing Work
outline.note: The teacher pictures his instruction as irrigation that becomes river and sea, then says his labor is for all who diligently seek wisdom.

keyVerses.text: Then the Creator of all things gave me a command. He who created me made my tent to rest, and said, ‘Let your dwelling be in Jacob, and your inheritance in Israel.’
keyVerses.why: This verse moves Wisdom from the whole created world into a specific dwelling among Jacob and Israel.

keyVerses.text: “Come to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits.
keyVerses.why: The chapter turns from Wisdom’s self-description to invitation, presenting Wisdom as something to be sought and received.

keyVerses.text: All these things are the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law which Moses commanded us for an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s clearest identification of Wisdom’s speech with the covenant law associated with Moses.

keyVerses.text: See that I have not labored for myself only, but for all those who diligently seek wisdom.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse presents the teacher’s work as public instruction, not private possession.

themes: Wisdom’s praise before the Most High

questions.question: Who is speaking in this chapter?
questions.answer: The opening verses introduce Wisdom as a female figure who praises herself and speaks among her people. In verses 3-22, Wisdom speaks in the first person, describing her origin, movement through creation, dwelling in Israel, and invitation to those who desire her. In the final section, the teacher connects this Wisdom with covenant law and with his own work of instruction.

questions.question: Does the chapter say Wisdom is everywhere or only in Israel?
questions.answer: It moves from a cosmic description of Wisdom to her dwelling in Israel. Wisdom covers the earth, moves through heaven, abyss, sea, earth, peoples, and nations, and then receives a command to dwell in Jacob and Israel. The chapter’s movement is from cosmic scope to a settled home in Zion and Jerusalem.

questions.question: What does “Most High” mean here?
questions.answer: “Most High” is the chapter’s title for God, the one before whom Wisdom speaks and from whose mouth Wisdom says she came. The chapter also calls God “the Creator of all things” and “the Most High God,” keeping Wisdom’s speech connected to God rather than making Wisdom an independent deity.

questions.question: What is the point of all the tree and fragrance comparisons?
questions.answer: Verses 13-17 use images of height, beauty, fragrance, branches, flowers, fruit, glory, and riches to describe Wisdom’s abundance and attractiveness. The comparisons do not define Wisdom as one object; they build a layered picture of something life-giving, honored, and desirable.

questions.question: Why are verses 18 and 24 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 18 and 24 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Is verse 23 saying Wisdom and the law are the same thing?
questions.answer: Verse 23 says, “All these things are the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law which Moses commanded us.” That directly links Wisdom’s self-praise with the covenant law. Readers may describe the relation differently: some speak of identification, while others emphasize that the poem presents Wisdom as concretely encountered through Torah and instruction.

questions.question: Why does Wisdom say eating and drinking lead to more hunger and thirst?
questions.answer: Verses 19-21 picture Wisdom as food and drink, but not as something exhausted by one meal. The point is that those who receive Wisdom desire more of her rather than finishing with her. The language is poetic, not a statement about physical hunger.

questions.question: Who is the “I” in verses 30-34?
questions.answer: The speaker appears to be the teacher reflecting on his own instruction. He compares his work to water moving from canal stream to garden, then river and sea, and says he will continue to pour out teaching. The final verse makes the purpose explicit: the labor is not for himself only, but for those who diligently seek wisdom.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader handle the grand claims about Wisdom’s age and existence?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says Wisdom was created “from the beginning, before the ages” and will not cease to exist. Interpreters debate how this language relates to later Jewish and Christian reflection on Wisdom, creation, Torah, and divine agency. Inside this chapter, the claim serves the poem’s main movement: Wisdom comes from God, fills creation, and is given a dwelling among Israel.

glossary.def: The personified speaker of the chapter, portrayed as coming from the Most High, moving through creation, dwelling in Israel, inviting seekers, and being linked with the covenant law.
A title for God in this chapter, used for the one before whom Wisdom speaks and from whose mouth Wisdom comes.
A holy worship setting named in the chapter; Wisdom says she ministered in the holy tabernacle, and later her fragrance is compared with frankincense in the tabernacle.
The phrase in verse 23 that connects Wisdom’s speech with the law Moses commanded for Jacob’s assemblies.
A repeated word for what is given and received: Wisdom’s dwelling in Israel and the law commanded as an inheritance for Jacob’s assemblies.
